cards.title: Three AI letters, three competing visions for US policy

panels.head: 235 companies vs. 1,324 researchers — AI's biggest policy fight is now public
panels.sub: Three open letters dropped in five days, each staking out a different position on open-weight models, distillation, and how fast AI should advance.

panels.head: Microsoft-led coalition: open weights are safer than closed ones
panels.sub: Signed July 24th by NVIDIA, Amazon, Y Combinator, Linux Foundation, and eventually OpenAI, the letter argues closed models create concentrated single points of failure. It explicitly defends distillation as a legitimate training technique, not misappropriation.

panels.head: Anthropic: distillation at industrial scale is the real threat
panels.sub: CEO Dario Amodei, writing three days later, stopped short of calling for an open-weights ban but pushed for cracking down on large-scale distillation operations and warned of authoritarian states building frontier models ahead of the US.

panels.head: 1,324 frontier-lab employees ask for a deliberate slowdown
panels.sub: Signatories including Anthropic's Amodei and OpenAI's chief scientist argue that AI-accelerated AI research creates runaway competitive pressure. The timing is pointed: Anthropic reports Claude Code writes 80% of their code; OpenAI cut serving costs 20% with automated optimisation.

panels.head: Distillation and open weights are the two policy levers that will reshape model access
panels.sub: If regulators restrict distillation, fine-tuning pipelines that rely on synthetic data from frontier models get legally complicated. PMs building on open-weight models in regulated industries should track this debate — the rules of the stack could shift within a legislative cycle.

cards.title: AFRL adds $11.7M to Blue Origin rocket cargo study

panels.head: The Air Force wants to ship cargo anywhere on Earth in under an hour
panels.sub: AFRL just added $11.7M to Blue Origin's existing contract to study whether orbital-class rockets can replace long-haul military cargo aircraft for time-critical deliveries.

panels.head: Point-to-point rocket cargo has been a USAF concept for years
panels.sub: The Rocket Cargo programme, launched around 2021, explores using commercial launch vehicles to deliver up to ~100 tonnes of supplies to any point on the globe in roughly 90 minutes — faster than any aircraft.

panels.head: Blue Origin joins SpaceX as a funded study partner
panels.sub: The expanded contract likely covers New Glenn as the candidate vehicle. SpaceX has a parallel agreement studying Starship for the same mission; AFRL is keeping multiple providers in the running.

panels.head: Military demand could de-risk reusable heavy-lift for everyone
panels.sub: If AFRL moves toward operational contracts, it creates a guaranteed revenue base that accelerates reusability and turnaround-time improvements — benefits that spill directly into commercial launch economics.

panels.head: Watch for an AFRL feasibility report, not a launch contract — yet
panels.sub: This is still a study phase. The key milestones to track are cost-per-kilogram estimates, basing logistics (rockets need launch infrastructure near conflict zones), and whether reuse rates can meet military surge demand.

cards.title: Space Force funds K2 laser comms demo at $22.9M

panels.head: Space Force hands K2 Space $22.9M to prove out laser links in orbit
panels.sub: The award funds a demonstration mission specifically targeting optical inter-satellite communications for military systems — not a study, an actual on-orbit test.

panels.head: Two satellites, two optical terminals
panels.sub: K2 will fly a pair of satellites each hosting a laser communications terminal, creating a real link to validate performance in the operational space environment.

panels.head: RF spectrum is congested and jammable; lasers are neither
panels.sub: Optical comms offer far higher bandwidth than radio, are harder to intercept or jam, and don't require spectrum licensing — three properties the military values heavily in contested environments.

panels.head: Space Force is diversifying its comms bets beyond legacy GEO satellites
panels.sub: This fits a broader push to proliferate resilient LEO mesh networks. K2 is a relatively young hardware startup, making this award a notable vote of confidence in new commercial providers.

panels.head: Watch for demo results as a readiness signal for optical ISL adoption
panels.sub: If K2's terminals hit latency and throughput targets on orbit, optical inter-satellite links become a near-term procurement option rather than a roadmap item — relevant to any edge compute or data-relay architecture tied to LEO.

cards.title: Datasette Agent can now smoke-test its own apps

panels.head: An AI agent that builds a web app and then tests it — without you lifting a finger
panels.sub: datasette-apps 0.2a0 ships two new tools that let Datasette Agent close its own feedback loop: build, inspect, fix.

panels.head: The trick: an invisible iframe the agent drives with JavaScript
panels.sub: app_debug() renders the app in an opacity-0, pointer-events-none iframe — hidden from the user — then executes agent-supplied JS inside it. The agent can verify functionality and even measure element dimensions.

panels.head: app_list() lets the agent find and edit apps it already owns
panels.sub: Rather than the user manually pointing the agent at an app, app_list() returns every app the current user has edit rights to — making iterative, multi-session editing practical.

panels.head: Both tools rely on context.browser_task() from datasette-agent 0.4a0
panels.sub: browser_task() is a new primitive that lets tool authors schedule sandboxed browser-side work from the agent context — the debug tool is the first real consumer of this API.

panels.head: Agentic coding loops just got a self-verification layer
panels.sub: The pattern — generate UI, render invisibly, run assertions, iterate — is one most AI coding tools skip entirely. Watching it land in an open-source data tool first is a useful proof-of-concept for any team building agent-driven front-end workflows.

cards.title: OpenAI's model cracks decade-old math problems

panels.head: Under $2,000 per unsolved math problem
panels.sub: OpenAI tasked an internal pre-release model with ten mathematical problems that had seen zero progress for at least a decade — and claims each solution cost less than $2,000 at GPT-5.6 Sol token prices.

panels.head: Lean 4 proofs published, paper included
panels.sub: The openai/ten-proofs repo contains formal Lean 4 verifications of the results, alongside a paper and an LLM-generated PDF reconstructing how each proof developed from unpublished reasoning traces.

panels.head: The scorecard has a blind spot
panels.sub: OpenAI reports cost-per-success but not cost-per-attempt. How many $2,000 runs ended without a solution? That denominator matters a lot for interpreting the headline figure.

panels.head: Mathematicians are having their Deep Blue moment
panels.sub: Terence Tao frames this as a shift toward 'big mathematics' — humans claim creative direction, AI handles technical grunt work at scale. One mathematician published an essay calling it a 'profound spiritual crisis.'

panels.head: The frontier is formal verification, not just generation
panels.sub: For PMs building AI reasoning pipelines: the publishable credibility here comes from Lean 4 — machine-checkable proofs, not just model-generated text. Pairing generation with formal verification is the pattern worth watching.
